original_value: Laser scanning data from unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV-LS) offer new opportunities to estimate forest growing stock volume (   V   ) exclusively based on the UAV-LS data. We propose a method to measure tree attributes and using these measurements to estimate    V    without the use of field data for calibration. The method consists of five steps: i) Using UAV-LS data, tree crowns are automatically identified and segmented wall-to-wall. ii) From all detected tree crowns, a sample is taken where diameter at breast height (DBH) can be recorded reliably as determined by visual assessment in the UAV-LS data. iii) Another sample of crowns is taken where tree species were identifiable from UAV image data. iv) DBH and tree species models are fit using the samples and applied to all detected tree crowns. v) Single tree volumes are predicted with existing allometric models using predicted species and DBH, and height directly obtained from UAV-LS. The method was applied to a Riegl-VUX data set with an average density of 1130 points m−2 and 3 cm orthomosaic acquired over an 8.8 ha managed boreal forest. The volumes of the identified trees were aggregated to estimate plot-, stand-, and forest-level volumes which were validated using 58 independently measured field plots. The root-mean-square deviance (    R M S  D %     ) decreased when increasing the spatial scale from the plot (32.2%) to stand (27.1%) and forest level (3.5%). The accuracy of the UAV-LS estimates varied given forest structure and was highest in open pine stands and lowest in dense birch or spruce stands. On the forest level, the estimates based on UAV-LS data were well within the 95% confidence interval of the intense field survey estimate, and both estimates had a similar precision. While the results are encouraging for further use of UAV-LS in the context of fully airborne forest inventories, future studies should confirm our findings in a variety of forest types and conditions.

result.paraphrase: Laser scanning data collected from unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV-LS) create new possibilities for estimating forest growing stock volume (V) using UAV-LS data alone. We present a method for measuring tree attributes and using those measurements to estimate V without any field data for calibration. The approach has five steps: i) tree crowns are automatically identified and segmented wall-to-wall from UAV-LS data; ii) a sample is drawn from the detected crowns where diameter at breast height (DBH) can be reliably recorded, based on visual assessment of the UAV-LS data; iii) another crown sample is selected where tree species can be identified from UAV image data; iv) DBH and tree-species models are fitted from the samples and applied to all detected tree crowns; v) single-tree volumes are predicted with existing allometric models using predicted species and DBH, while height is obtained directly from UAV-LS. The method was tested on a Riegl-VUX data set with an average density of 1130 points m−2 and a 3 cm orthomosaic acquired over 8.8 ha of managed boreal forest. Volumes for the identified trees were summed to estimate plot-, stand-, and forest-level volumes and were validated against 58 independently measured field plots. Root-mean-square deviance (RMSD%) declined as spatial scale increased, from the plot level (32.2%) to the stand level (27.1%) and the forest level (3.5%). Accuracy of the UAV-LS estimates depended on forest structure and was best in open pine stands and poorest in dense birch or spruce stands. At forest scale, the UAV-LS-based estimates fell well within the 95% confidence interval of the intensive field survey estimate, and both approaches showed similar precision. Although the results are promising for broader use of UAV-LS in fully airborne forest inventories, further studies should verify these findings across a range of forest types and conditions.
